hook_clip: Here's how to reverse engineer Guru from a written spec. Claude passed all thirty-one checks, and found thirty gaps in my spec.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: We gave Claude one Markdown file. It copies the part of Guru a small team actually needs to stop answering the same questions in Slack. Every answer is a card, with one owner. Each card says whether it's verified, and when it needs review. Anyone can flag a wrong answer. And every edit is a new version, with a note saying what changed.

The core rule is trust. It's never stored. It's worked out every time a card is shown. A card turns unverified when its owner leaves, when someone flags it, when someone else edits it, or when its review date passes. Sam Okafor edits Ben's card on software purchases, so it waits for Ben to verify it.

Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. The foundation, with people, teams, collections and sign-in. Cards, trust and flags. Search, insights and the export. Then notifications, review reminders and a Slack command. After every phase, the acceptance checks ran in a real browser, from fresh seed data.

Here's what it built. The VPN card shows who verified it, when it's next due, and what changed. Searching for laptop puts the verified card ahead of one whose owner has left. Insights shows six of ten cards verified, sixty percent, and who needs to review what. Ben's cards list the ones he must check first. And Compare shows the old VPN steps against the new ones, line by line.
In one final run, on a fresh database, all thirty-one checks passed, along with one hundred and fifty-five automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The build exposed thirty gaps in the spec. Places where Claude had to guess. Nothing said whether the last admin could be deactivated. Search could turn the word does into doe, because the spec never said when to remove stop words. And a card with a channel-wide mention could notify everyone in a Slack channel. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't the same as production-ready. We didn't test production sign-in, real email delivery, a real Slack workspace, the hourly job on a real scheduler, or hosting. Those are yours to check before your team relies on it.

So is it worth building? Guru doesn't publish prices. Its pricing page says the cost is tailored to your organization, and scoped on a call with its team. If you want AI answers drawn from Google Drive, Confluence and Slack, or controls like SSO and SOC two, talk to Guru. If you just need one owned, current answer to every question your team keeps asking, build it.
Everything is in one file. The data model, nineteen rules, seed data, four phase prompts, and all thirty-one checks, with the thirty fixes already in.
